title: The Sunpetal's Gift
markdown:
In the sun-drenched Whispering Canyons, where wind wrote secrets into sandstone and thermals rose like lazy spirits, Vita lived with her head full of sky. She was an apprentice pilot. Her days were engines and currents, and Remy, the orchard mechanic whose hands could talk a tired machine back into usefulness. Their prize was the Sunpetal, a glider they had restored together through a winter of resin, thread, and arguments about rivets. Remy had taught Vita that a wing wants honesty more than bravery. Vita had taught Remy that a sky-chart is a kind of kindness you can fold. Its wings, patched with cloud-silk, held the light as if light liked them. On quiet evenings they rolled the glider out just to hear the fabric speak.

One crisp morning, rose and gold on the canyon walls, a runner came in with worry worn into his face.

“The Sunpetal must fly,” he said. “Old Man Hemlock’s camp, in the forgotten orchards. His granddaughter Lily needs a fracture splint. Her leg is broken, and a cough has settled in her chest.”

Vita’s heart went quick. This was not a delivery. This was a child, and a clock she could already hear. Remy’s brow furrowed in that way that made the lines around his eyes kinder, not harder.

“The Sunpetal is ready,” he said. “Its heart is sound. Its wings want sky.”

They launched before the runner’s dust had settled. Vita wanted the short line, the heroic one, the line that made a story of itself. Remy glanced at the peaks and said nothing yet. The glider took the morning thermals with a sigh that sounded almost pleased. Vita’s fingers were light on the controls. Remy sat beside her, a quiet weight, a bag of tools knocking softly against the rib. Below them the orchards unrolled green, rivers like silver thread. A hawk hung in a thermal they were stealing, and did not seem to mind.

Near the Obsidian Peaks the air changed its mind. Remy said, “Wide,” and Vita, hearing Lily’s cough instead, took the notch. A downdraft hit as sharp as a hawk. The Sunpetal lurched, shuddered, and tumbled. Vita’s first instinct was to fight the stick as if will could flatten weather.

“Hold on,” Remy said, calm enough to be an insult to the wind.

They put down in a controlled crash among scrubby pine. Crushed needles filled the air. Miles short. Vita tasted metal. She had rushed the line through the peaks because Lily’s cough had been louder in her head than the air. The glider sat among the trees looking offended and smaller.

They dusted pine resin from their suits and saw a smoke-stained hut clinging to the mountainside. A grizzled man came out with a gnarled staff that might have grown from his own arm.

“What business do you have disturbing my peace?” he asked. His eyes were sharp and unused to company.

This was Silas. People in the canyons spoke of him the way they spoke of locked sheds: useful, perhaps, and not to be leaned on.

Vita explained. She kept her voice clear. A child. A splint. A cough. Silas’s face did not soften.

“A splint,” he said. “And what makes you think I have such a thing to spare?” He gestured at the hut, its one window like a suspicious eye. “The world outside has taken enough. I trust no one. Not the wind. Not the rain. And not people who arrive with stories.”

Remy stepped forward before Vita’s impatience could do the talking.

“Sir,” he said, gentle, measured. “Her name is Lily. She is very small. We can offer you what we have.”

Silas chuckled, dry as leaves on stone. “Anything? Your grand glider, then. The Sunpetal. It will fetch a price in the South Pass markets. Enough peace for a season.” He pointed to the battered frame in the pines. “Give me that machine and you may have your splint. Trust is a fool’s currency. Kindness comes back as theft.”

The offer sat in the air like a second downdraft. Vita nearly said yes. Lily’s clock was loud. The Sunpetal was wood and silk; a child was a child. She felt the words lining up. Then she saw the wear on Remy’s face, felt the mountain wind find the gaps in her suit, and the yes caught. Trading the glider would get a splint and lose the only way home that was faster than walking. It was the sort of bargain her hurry loved, and it was a bad one.

She looked at the Sunpetal: hours of patching, laughter in the hangar, the belief they had stitched into the wings. She looked at Remy. She looked at Silas properly, past the leather of his suspicion, and saw a man who had been kind once and had decided kindness was a hole.

From her flight bag she took the thing she loved more than polished fittings: a sky-chart drawn by her own hand. Constellations. Wind-roads. Secret paths she had found by not quite following the safe ones. The parchment smelled of old ink.

“Take this,” she said. The wind pulled at the edges. “It will not buy you a season in the markets. It is the sky I know. If you want something that is not a demand, here it is.”

Silas blinked. He looked from the lines to her face. He reached out. His fingers, stiff from years of holding the world off, traced a current she had marked in a careful hand. A sigh left him that sounded like a long-closed door noticing it still had hinges.

“You offer beauty,” he said, quieter, “when I expected a hand in my stores. Perhaps the world is not entirely out of gentle souls.”

He went into the hut. The door complained. He came back with a bundle tied in twine. Inside lay a splint of pale willow, lightning-struck wood, smooth and strong, the sort of work a lonely man does when he still remembers how to make a thing well.

They spent an hour on the Sunpetal before they trusted it with sky again. Remy spliced a rib. Vita walked the fabric with her palms, finding the places the pine had kissed too hard. A thermal tried the wreck and moved on, disappointed. When they rose, they took the long way around the teeth of the peaks, and the glider, patched again, took the air without being asked to be a hero.

At Hemlock’s camp the air smelled of woodsmoke and waiting. Old Man Hemlock’s hands shook when he saw the willow. Remy set the splint as if he were fitting a wing. Vita held the lamp and told Lily, who was very small and very hot, about a hawk that had shared their thermal. Lily’s fever broke in the days that followed. Her lullabies came back, small and off-key and alive. The cough loosened its claim.

They visited, not as couriers who had dropped a parcel, but as people who had sat in a hut and watched a man decide not to stay entirely shut. They spoke of Silas without making him a lesson. They left him his name and his smoke. Once they left a basket of early apples on his step and did not knock. The basket was gone by evening. The step, they noticed, had been swept.

Months later the Sunpetal rode a late afternoon thermal, gold along the wings. Vita looked down. A thin wisp rose from the hermit’s hut, a pale thread against a great deal of blue. She did not read it as a warning. She read it as a kettle, perhaps, or a man who had opened a chart and found a reason to keep a fire.

The next time a runner came with a clock in his voice, Vita still felt the pull to go now, now, now. She checked the wind first, then the silk, then Remy’s face. Remy, tightening a line, did not have to tell her. They took the wide road around the peaks, and arrived later than a legend would have liked, and in time enough. The canyon, which had always been loud with air, made a little room for that.
